KEY MESSAGE 1...Showers and thunderstorms increase in coverage 
tonight into Monday with the potential for areas of heavy rain 
leading to a risk of flash flooding. There is also some risk for
strong to severe thunderstorms.

An upper-level trough is moving into the Northeast through
Monday. As this trough moves into the Northeast, there will be 
plenty of upper-level energy moving through the region. There is
also a warm air advection set up into tonight. For Monday, 
there will be a jet streak overhead with our location in the 
right entrance region. All of these factors will lead to a 
period of unsettled weather in the near term.

As we head into tonight, an increasing south to southwest flow will 
continue to bring in increasing moisture with PWAT values tonight 
surging to 2+ inches tonight. The coverage of showers and 
thunderstorms will also be increasing with the warm air 
advection regime allowing for an increase in ascent. Overnight, 
instability will also be increasing, but the timing is not very 
supportive of severe weather. Through tonight, there is a 
Marginal (level 1 out of 4) risk for excessive rainfall. Model 
soundings continue to show this risk into tonight as well with 
the high PWATs and warm cloud layer processes. 

On Monday, a cold front will be approaching the region. There 
continues to be a signal for ripples of energy along the front. 
Also, in the upper-levels, a jet streak will be overhead with our 
area in the right entrance region which allows for additional 
forcing and ascent for our area. Showers and thunderstorms look to 
be ongoing into tomorrow morning with an increase in the coverage 
again during the afternoon and evening. 

As PWATs continue to remain above 2 inches ahead of the front, the 
risk for heavy rain continues. The overall flow will be weaker 
tomorrow with training and slow moving storms being a concern 
leading to the heavy rainfall risk. There is a slight (level 2 out 
of 4) for excessive rainfall for tomorrow for areas near and east 
of the I-95 corridor. The remainder of the area is in a Maringal 
(level 1 out of 4) risk for excessive rainfall. Due to the risk for 
heavy rainfall tonight and into tomorrow, a Flood Watch has been 
issued for the I-95 corridor, northern NJ, and the Lehigh Valley for 
the potential of rainfall rates of 1-3 inches per hour. Rainfall 
amounts of 1-2 inches are possible with localized amounts to 3-5 
inches. This Flood Watch is in effect from 8 PM this evening until 
11 PM Monday.

In terms of the severe weather risk tomorrow, uncertainty remains 
around the exact extent of instability present due to cloud cover 
and the round of showers/thunderstorms around tomorrow morning. If 
enough heating develops during the course of the day, then this 
combined with some increase in shear ahead of the front could lead 
to at least some severe thunderstorm risk. The Storm Prediction 
Center has highlighted areas near and northwest of the I-95 corridor 
in a Marginal risk (level 1 out of 5) for isolated severe 
thunderstorms with the primary risk being damaging wind gusts.


KEY MESSAGE 2...A warm front is expected to lift through the region 
Tuesday Night into Wednesday, bringing the next chance for showers 
and storms.

Once the current system gets east of our region, the next thing to 
watch is a warm front slowly lifting north over our region. The most 
likely time period for this frontal passage is Tuesday night into 
Wednesday, leaving the day time on Tuesday relatively dry. However, 
at least one model is showing a very fast warm frontal passage with 
the front north of our region by late Wednesday Night. In this fast 
solution, the pattern is odd, depicting a very pronounced mid and 
upper level short wave ridge in place throughout the day. This 
pattern isn't favorable for fast frontal passages. Therefore, have 
favored the blend of guidance, which favors the slower solution.

As far as hazards, the primary hazard is likely to be heavy rain 
leading to flash flooding. There will likely be significant low 
level moisture advection behind the front, increasing the risk for 
heavy rain. That combined with the fact that storm motions are 
likely to be quite slow (less than 20 mph), increases the risk for 
flash flooding. One factor which we won't know until late Monday is 
how much antecedent conditions will play a role in the flash 
flooding threat - areas that get heavy rain through the day on 
Monday will have little opportunity for the water to drain before 
this next round of rain chances.

The severe threat is less clear. This will be dependent on the 
timing of the front - if the frontal passage, and thus prime period 
for any showers and storms is during the daylight hours when 
instability is maximized, there will be some threat for damaging 
winds. Some model soundings show a very dry mid layer, increasing 
the threat for downbursts.
